Welcome to CityChats, where Brisbane Times meets our city's most interesting characters on our most iconic form of transport. This week, Graya co-founder and managing director Rob Gray tells us how he thinks the city should tackle the housing crisis, what Brisbane 2032 will mean for construction prices, and the suburbs Graya has its eye on.

We meet Gray at Teneriffe ferry stop, just a short walk from his head office. He's immediately recognisable in a Graya branded T-shirt. As we cruise along the Brisbane River, we spot multiple Graya-branded signs at prime real estate spots in the city's most affluent areas.

What's your controversial Brisbane opinion?

I think, personally, we have a little bit of a housing crisis at the moment. Houses are really expensive; rents are really expensive. What would really help would be going up and not out. Potentially lifting some height limits in the busy areas would really help everybody.

In a perfect world, if money wasn't an object and you could do whatever you want, what would be your dream Brisbane project?

This is going to sound corny, but I think the dream Brisbane projects I'm already doing. You know, from riverfront developments in Saint Lucia, to restaurants and retail developments in Racecourse Road and James Street, it's things that I've always wanted to do. Maybe the next thing I really want to be part of is the Brisbane skyline.

What inspired you to get into development?

From a very young age, I always wanted to get into property development. I just really loved doing things with my hands. I loved creating something. I like the fulfillment, seeing something come out of the ground and be able to experience the hard work.

There are whole areas in Brisbane that Graya is really reshaping. Do you feel it's a big responsibility, and how have you dealt with that?

I think as Graya has matured as a business, I am starting to feel more responsibility to the Brisbane community that we need to do a really good job.

Especially now, because we've moved out of individual homes and now we're doing what we like to call lifestyle developments. We like to bring in the retail and fashion and restaurants. It's putting a huge responsibility on us to make our city great.

You've had an enormous amount of success in quite a short period of time in what's very famously a hugely cutthroat industry. What's the secret behind your success and your rapid growth?

It might look like it's quite quick from the outside in, but for us, it's been quite slow. But we've been really determined from the outset to do a really good product, so we really focused on that for a long period of time.

And you look back over a decade and a half, and you really have done a lot of things.

Graya's got a really distinctive aesthetic and style. How did that come about? Is there a building in Brisbane you're particularly proud of?

I think we're really fortunate in Brisbane, we've got such a good climate - it's not too cold, it's not too hot -
title: Graya's co-founder on how to tackle the city's housing crisis
author: WAtoday

The rising cost of living in Lagos is forcing a difficult question into everyday conversations: must Nigerians remain in the commercial capital to build successful careers, businesses and comfortable lives?

That debate has intensified after Lagos State Deputy Governor Obafemi Hamzat advised young workers struggling with high rents to consider staying with their parents or relatives, or sharing accommodation until they can afford to live independently. His comments drew mixed reactions online, with some Nigerians describing the suggestion as practical and others arguing that it underestimated the financial pressures already confronting young workers.

The frustration is backed by a wider squeeze on housing costs. Nigeria's annual rent inflation jumped to 33.74 per cent in July 2026 from 14.79 per cent in June, according to National Bureau of Statistics data reported by Nairametrics, even as headline inflation moderated to 15.43 per cent.

Brandspur Brand News reports that the situation is reopening discussion about whether professionals, young families and entrepreneurs whose work does not require them to remain permanently in Lagos could achieve a better quality of life in smaller Nigerian cities, satellite towns and less congested communities.

Housing sits at the centre of the argument. In parts of Lagos, rent increases have moved far ahead of wages. Reporting on the city's housing crisis earlier this year found examples of Mainland apartments that rented for about ₦500,000 two years earlier reaching as much as ₦2.5 million annually, while some workers have moved farther from their workplaces simply to secure accommodation they can afford.

But cheaper housing outside the city's busiest districts can create another bill: transport. One worker living in Sango Ota, Ogun State, while working on Lagos Island described a commute stretching to about four hours. It captures the trade-off many workers face -- pay more to live closer to work or spend less on rent and surrender hours of each day to commuting.

That is where smaller towns can become attractive, particularly for remote workers, freelancers, digital entrepreneurs, retirees and business owners whose customers are not concentrated in Lagos.

Lower housing costs can leave more money available for food, savings, children's education, business expansion or emergencies. Reduced congestion may also mean shorter journeys and less money spent repeatedly on fuel, ride-hailing services or public transport.

There is also the question of time. Lagos remains Nigeria's biggest commercial centre and offers enormous opportunities, but accessing those opportunities can come with long hours in traffic. A 2026 traffic ranking placed Lagos as Africa's most congested city, with an estimated average one-way commute of about 68 minutes.

For someone whose income can be earned from a laptop, online shop, consulting service or remotely managed business, paying a premium simply to remain close to Lagos' commercial
title: Lagos Is Too Expensive: Why Smaller Nigerian Towns Are Back In The

As September 11th approaches, the date will bring up lots of memories.

Most people can recall where they were on that day 25 years ago. It's a historic event that has left its mark, has changed societies and the way we live.

Among the many lives lost in the attacks were 343 members of the New York City Fire Department (NYFD).

They ran towards danger while others were trying to escape it.

West Cork plays an important role in commemorating those brave souls.

Near Kinsale, the Garden of Remembrance provides a quiet and respectful place to remember them.

Situated on private land, it is maintained by a dedicated group of volunteers whose work ensures that the garden remains cared for and welcoming to visitors.

In contrast to metal plaques or stone monuments, the garden is a living memorial, with a tree dedicated to each of the firefighters.

A serene and peaceful place that changes through the seasons.

Its initiator, Kathleen Cait Murphy, made a gift to the families and friends of the 9/11 deceased and the wider West Cork community.

Over the years, the garden has become well-known far beyond Ireland.

Visitors from the US and other parts of the world come to see it and take a moment to sit and reflect.

Its reputation crosses borders and helps to bring people together.

Political administrations have come and gone in both countries but the annual commemoration at Ringfinnan remains a steady fixture in the calendar.

As former FDNY firefighter Danny Manning, one of the garden's chief advocates, put it: it's a place where party politics are left at the gate.

A fitting description of a memorial centred on remembrance, community and respect rather than the politics of loss and grief.

The garden also highlights the long and personal relationship between Ireland and the US.

That relationship is based on much more than political or economic ties.

It has been built through families, migration, friendship and shared traditions.

The links between Kinsale and New York have been strengthened by the garden and by the people who visit, support and care for it.

Anyone who has visited will know there is a whole world of Irish life in New York, visible at St Patrick's Day parades, in Gaelic football and hurling clubs, music sessions -- and the FDNY.

These traditions remain a lively part of the city, connecting generations across the pond and maintaining a strong sense of community.

The Garden of Remembrance is part of that wider connection.

At a time when political debate is dominated by Donald Trump, who will be visiting Ireland next week, the focus is too often on division.

But the garden offers something different. It shows what can be achieved through co-operation, remembrance and personal relationships.

Its importance lies in its simplicity.

A local group, working on private land, has created and maintained a memorial known across the world. How lucky we are to have it?

Hope of a home fades

title: EDITORIAL: Kinsale 9/11 event a steady fixture

FIRST-TIME buyers in Cork now need to earn €92,092 to purchase a home, new research shows.

The sobering statistic shows the price of getting a foot on the property ladder in the Rebel County is significantly higher than the national average.

Cork has the highest income requirement in the south of the country, and is the only county outside of Dublin and its neighbouring commuter belt (Kildare, Meath and Wicklow) to need a salary above €90,000.

Even more worrying, the research from Chill Insurance shows that the median income for Cork is €46,416 - leaving a gap of €45,676 between what a single first-time buyer earns and what they need in order to purchase a house.

The research compared the median first-time buyer home price in each county, using the Residential Property Price Index as published by the Central Statistics Office (CSO), with median local incomes from CSO earnings data.

These figures were then assessed against the standard Central Bank lending rules, under which a buyer can borrow up to 90% of a home's value and up to four times their gross income.

The picture in Cork is bleak, with a typical first-time buyer home priced at €409,299, the county's median income estimated at €46,416, but the salary needed to qualify for a mortgage almost double that at €92,092.

Economist Austin Hughes said: 'The Chill report emphasises the nature of the problem would-be homebuyers face.

Even allowing for ongoing wage growth, in no county is the typical first-time buyer property accessible at present to the median wage-earner, unless they are in a position to get additional financial support from the State and/or their family.

'With would-be buyers in Cork now needing almost twice the typical wage and those in Dublin needing more than double the average wage, this purchase gap is growing and spreading in a worrisome manner.'

Director of sales and operations at Chill Insurance, Ian O'Reilly, noted: 'In Cork, a single buyer earning the local median income would still not earn enough to borrow what they need for a typical first home. For many first-time buyers, closing that gap means saving a larger deposit, buying with another person or looking at State supports such as the First Home Scheme or the Local Authority Home Loan.'

The findings come as the latest figures for those in emergency accommodation points to a deepening housing crisis which is being felt across Cork.

Figures released by the Department of Housing last Friday show there were 820 adults in emergency accommodation in Cork in July - an increase of 27% on July 2025 and up 48% on July 2024.

Nationally, more than 17,500 people were living in emergency accommodation in July, including 5,659 children.

The latest report from charity Depaul shows a growing demand for homeless services across Cork city and county.

Its 2025 impact report outlines a year of progress, against a backdrop of rising demand for its support services.

Across its Cork services last year Depaul supported 512 pe
title: Cork buyers need a €92k salary in order to purchase a house
author: The Southern Star

Fresh plans are being developed for a new community of around 3,500 homes between York and Selby.

Escrick Park Estate is progressing plans for Heronby on land west of Escrick, with proposals also expected to include schools, a health centre, country park and other community facilities.

An early masterplan for the development was prepared as part of the former Selby Local Plan process in 2021.

However, that process stalled and was subsequently halted after North Yorkshire Council took over responsibility for planning in the area following local government reorganisation in 2023.

Escrick Park Estate has now confirmed it is working towards submitting an outline planning application for the development.

As part of that process, an environmental impact assessment scoping request has been submitted to North Yorkshire Council.

The request is not itself a planning application. Instead, it asks council officers to determine what environmental issues will need to be examined in an environmental statement accompanying a future application.

The developers say the proposals are being revived in response to North Yorkshire's shortage of planned new housing.

Beilby Forbes Adam, of Escrick Park Estate, said the estate had remained committed to the project despite the previous local plan process ending.

"Two years later we are moving closer to being ready to submit an outline application," he said.

"But before we do we want to hear what the potential future residents of Heronby would like to see there."

Mr Forbes Adam said the consultation was open to all ages but the team particularly wanted younger people to get involved, referring to those struggling to find homes of their own as "Generation Limbo".

"The housing crisis means too many young people can't find a home of their own and are struggling to get on and lead their own lives," he added.

"We want to hear from 'Generation Limbo'."

Selby councillor, Steve Shaw-Wright, said there was a lot of support for the proposal among councillors in the former Selby district when the plans were first discussed.

"It would, if you like, mop up all the developments that were planned for the Selby area at the time.

"Instead of having bits and bobs of development in each village causing uproar, you would have this large development that would be like a new village with a school, a medical centre and everything else you need.

"It just seemed to be a sensible solution to the long-term housing issues that we've got in Selby."

But Councillor John Cattanach, who represents the Cawood and Escrick division, including the site of the proposed development, is opposed to the plans.

He said: "Since the inception, I've spoken out against it completely and utterly -- it's complete madness. It's the size of the development and where it is, and the fact that all these people would go on to the A19."

A public exhibition is planned in Escrick later this year, while initial proposals and a feedback form are available on the
title: Heronby: Fresh plans revealed for 3,500 homes between York and Selby
author: Yorkshire Post

ESC Homes' permit-ready ADU plans are sized to clear each Virginia county's limits, built for aging parents, adult children and multigenerational households

A parent who needs to be close, but not in the guest room. A disabled family member who needs their own door. Three generations negotiating one kitchen. Nobody was building for any of that."

-- Cheryl Spangler, Owner, ESC Homes

GAINESVILLE, VA, UNITED STATES, September 8, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- GAINESVILLE, Va. -- Sept. 8, 2026 -- When Virginia's new accessory dwelling unit law takes effect on July 1, 2027, homeowners across the Commonwealth will be able to add a second, independent dwelling to their property by right in single-family zones, with ADU permit fees capped at $500 and no requirement that occupants be related by family.

That last provision -- the removal of the family-relation requirement -- points at who these units are actually for.

"After more than twenty years of listening to buyers, the same conversations kept repeating," said Cheryl Spangler, owner of ESC Homes. "An adult child who can't find rent she can cover. A parent who needs to be close, but not in the guest room. A disabled family member who needs their own door. Three generations negotiating one kitchen. Nobody was building for any of that."

ESC Homes, a Northern Virginia builder focused exclusively on small-footprint homes and ADUs, is telling homeowners the same thing it tells its own clients: the deadline is not the starting line.

"Design, permitting, financing, and contractor selection take months before anyone breaks ground," Spangler said. "Homeowners who wait until July 2027 to make a phone call are looking at 2028 before they have a finished unit. The people who will benefit first from this law are the ones planning right now."

ESC Homes builds five architectural collections across a range of floorplans, each able to serve as a primary residence or an ADU. The range is deliberate: Virginia counties set their own ADU size limits, and a plan that clears review in one jurisdiction can be too large in the next. The plans are permit-ready, so county review can begin immediately rather than after months of custom architectural work.

The homes are stick-built on permanent foundations with a four-foot crawlspace -- not modular units or structures on trailers, and they follow conventional paths for appraisal, financing, and resale.

ESC Homes' plans use elevated ceiling heights and clerestory windows -- a signature of the company's work -- to make compact interiors read as open and light-filled.

"Small footprint has been shorthand for cheap and temporary for too long," Spangler said. "Thinking small doesn't have to mean living small. Volume, natural light, and proportion are what make a space feel generous, and none of those are a function of square footage."

Spangler came to homebuilding from the other side of the transaction. Licensed in Virginia real estate since 2002 and a brokerage owner, she has s
title: Virginia ADU Law 2027: ESC Homes Offers Permit-Ready Solutions

The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Fame Oyster & Co., Mr Olufemi Oyedele, has urged the Federal Government to abandon attempts to regulate cement prices, arguing that Nigeria's housing crisis is rooted in a faulty building production system rather than the activities of cement manufacturers.

Oyedele's position comes amid growing calls for the relevant committees of the National Assembly to summon cement manufacturers, regulators and distributors to explain the pricing chain following the sharp increase in the price of cement.

A 50-kilogramme bag of cement currently sells for about N15,000 in some markets, adding to the cost pressures confronting prospective homeowners and developers amid Nigeria's huge housing deficit.

But Oyedele said regulating the price of cement without addressing the country's overdependence on the material could prove counterproductive.

"Our problem is not the cement manufacturers but the fact that our building production system is wrong," he said.

He called on the government to establish a committee to examine alternative building materials and construction technologies that could reduce Nigerians' dependence on cement.

According to him, Nigeria has abundant natural resources and construction waste that could be converted into affordable building materials, but these opportunities remain largely untapped.

Oyedele said the country's dependence on sandcrete blocks, which are mainly produced from Portland cement, had contributed significantly to the rising cost of building construction.

He urged stakeholders to look beyond cement and explore materials that are cheaper, locally available and environmentally sustainable.

He cited the United States, where materials such as natural wood siding, brick masonry, vinyl siding, fibre-cement siding, stone, metal siding and composite cladding are widely used in building construction.

READ ALSO: FCCPC and the suspected cement price manipulators

He said Nigeria could similarly develop and promote alternative materials suited to its environment and local resources.

Oyedele also identified construction and demolition waste as a major opportunity for reducing building costs.

He said a large proportion of materials generated as waste on Nigerian construction sites could be recovered, processed and reused instead of being dumped.

"While a serious prospective homeowner can conveniently build a two-bedroom flat from construction waste around Nigeria, demolition waste is not recycled or reused for construction," he said.

He estimated that about 34 per cent of construction costs in Nigeria goes into construction waste, describing the situation as a major source of inefficiency in the industry.

He cited construction waste dumps at Oniru in Victoria Island, Lagos, and the Ogere Industrial Area along the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway as examples of the enormous quantity of waste generated by the construction sector.

title: Housing crisis: Fix building system, not cement prices -- Oyedele

The divergence in China's economy became even more pronounced over the past quarter as consumer demand weakened further while export growth reached new heights and tech keeps booming.

We expect this two-speed economy to continue for the rest of 2026 and into 2027.

China's housing crisis is a key factor behind the ongoing consumer slump. We see signs of stabilization in home sales and look for home prices to stabilize in 2027.

We have lowered the GDP growth forecast for 2026 from 4.8% to 4.6% on the back of the disappointing consumer data in recent months. We stick to our forecast of 4.7% for 2027.

China's tech boom pushes the economy into new frontiers. The rising competitive pressure from China for European companies is set to continue. EU and China are on collision course in trade relations.

We look for China to keep a 'CNY appreciation policy' over the coming year.

The US and China have agreed on 'constructive strategic stability' but bumps in the road are ongoing and a long-term rivalry is here to stay.

The biggest geopolitical risk related to China is a flare-up in tensions over Taiwan. 2028 elections on Taiwan will be a key test.

CJP seeks accountability, safer student housing, compensation and structural audits after seven people died in Delhi.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has issued seven demands after a five-storey paying guest (PG) building in Delhi's Satya Niketan collapsed, killing seven people, most of them students.

CJP spokesperson Saurav Das has sought an independent criminal probe into an alleged nexus between PG owners, politicians and others, along with engineering-grade structural audits, a public database of safe student accommodation, more government hostels, compensation of ₹1 crore for each deceased victim's family and ₹20 lakh for every injured person.

The party has also sought records of 13 district committees formed to inspect buildings and fix ministerial accountability, specifically questioning the role of Delhi's Urban Development, Planning and Education Minister Ashish Sood. Meanwhile, the Delhi High Court has ordered a high-level MCD inquiry, while five MCD officials have been suspended amid growing scrutiny over building-safety enforcement.

Seven Demands For Accountability

CJP's demands come a day after the Satya Niketan tragedy, where a privately operated boys' PG building collapsed, leaving seven people dead and several others injured. The party has called for an investigation that goes beyond the property owner and examines what Das described as the "larger PG mafia". He said the alleged links between property owners, politicians and people in positions of power must also be examined.

The organisation has also demanded time-bound, "engineering-grade" structural audits of student accommodation, schools and colleges, followed by action against unsafe or unauthorised structures. It wants the government to create a publicly searchable database showing whether student accommodation is legally sanctioned and structurally safe.

Another key demand is for adequate government hostels for Delhi University and other students. Das said DU currently has hostel capacity for around 7,000 students, despite its student population running into lakhs. "Student accommodation cannot be left to unsafe private PGs alone," the CJP said in its seven-point charter.

From Compensation To Ministerial Accountability

CJP has sought ₹1 crore for each family that lost a loved one and ₹20 lakh for every injured victim. It has also demanded that records of 13 district committees formed after the June 3 Hauz Rani incident be made public within 48 hours, including their inspection, enforcement and sealing records. The party alleges that these committees became inactive within months and wants clarity on whether Satya Niketan was inspected and what action, if any, followed.

The seventh demand directly concerns political accountability. Das has named Ashish Sood, Delhi's Urban Development, Planning and Education Minister, asking why the work of the district committees was allegedly wound down and who authorised it. "Accountability must be fixed for him," Das said, argu
title: Satya Niketan Tragedy: What are CJP's 7 Demands? Seeks PG Safety Audits, Govt Hostels And Accountability - The Logical Indian
author: The Logical Indian

One councillor branded the situation a 'tragedy'

There are fears an apparent housing crisis in Stockport is 'out of control'. Between 2020 and 2025, the number of people presenting to Stockport council as homeless has increased by 1,155 - up 72 per cent.

Between 2019 and 2025 the number of people rough sleeping has quadrupled. Figures show Stockport is now only behind Manchester in Greater Manchester. Some £2m has been spent on temporary accommodation.

While the A Bed Every Night scheme does provide emergency accommodation, there is currently a waiting list.

Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter

The most common reasons for homelessness are either family or friends no longer willing or able to accommodate people; the end of a private rented tenancy; those leaving Home Office accommodation; and domestic abuse.

The local authority said that as a result of demand, it has seen a 'sharp rise' in hotels and bed and breakfasts being used 'due to insufficient supply of suitable alternatives'.

In a Stockport council report, councillor Jake Austin, who oversees the council's service, said homelessness 'remains one of the most pressing challenges facing our communities', adding: "These challenges have led to record levels of homelessness presentations."

To tackle the problem, the council said it will increase early intervention and support. On housing, a council report said the local authority would look to improve access to the private rented sector, support people to maintain their tenancies, and promote safety.

At a meeting on September 3, Labour councillor Claire Vibert said: "The housing crisis is becoming out of control in Stockport. It's getting worse and worse every year." She argued there was no 'genuine ambition' by the council to resolve the issue.

Pointing to the council's regeneration plans for the town centre, she said: "We are doing things now where we could make active decisions to solve or significantly alleviate the issues within Stockport."

In response, Coun Austin said temporary accommodation costs were high even if lower than expected and they were looking at opportunities to reduce them. He also said the Labour UK government needed to get more of a grip on the issue and provide more funding.

He told councillors: "What you described as a Stockport crisis is probably better described as a national housing crisis. We are certainly not the only council within the country. In fact, almost all councils around the country are facing the same issue."

Green councillor James Frizzell said there needed to be more social housing built and criticised the national picture, adding: "There have been things coming down the track which are now hitting us so hard, hitting these vulnerable families, and this could been done a long time ago. This is political failure."

Concerns were also raised about the continuation of a policy housing homeless families outside of the borough including as far awa
title: Fears a crisis in Stockport is 'out of control'
author: Manchester Evening News

A proposed new Woollahra station could anchor thousands of new apartments, more open space and improved walking paths under a new draft plan.

The NSW government has released the draft rezoning plan for Woollahra and Edgecliff, potentially delivering up to 9400 new homes.

The plan covers 168 hectares in Sydney's east and sets out how the area could change over the next 20 years, with new housing, jobs, open space and walking and cycling links planned around public transport.

The proposal comes as the NSW government plans for Sydney to accommodate at least 800,000 additional homes and 950,000 more jobs by 2046. The state's Sydney Plan directs more housing towards established areas in the east, close to jobs, public transport and essential services, while identifying western Sydney as a major focus for economic growth.

The Woollahra and Edgecliff plan follows NSW premier Chris Minns' announcement in August 2025 that the state would finally complete the abandoned Woollahra station and rezone the area to increase housing density. The facility was partially built in 1970s before being ditched due to community pressure.

The new local plan is centred on the existing Edgecliff station and a proposed new Woollahra station, which the government expects to be operational in 2029. Woollahra station would connect to the T4 Eastern Suburbs Line, with a trip to the Sydney CBD expected to take about eight minutes.

The most significant residential development would be concentrated around the two stations, with building heights of up to 34 storeys proposed around Edgecliff Station and up to 32 storeys around Woollahra Station.

Up to 40% of new dwellings would be located within 200 metres of a train station, according to the NSW government.

Mr Minns said established suburbs needed to make a fair contribution to Sydney's housing growth.

"For the last decade, we've asked a small number of communities to carry the lion's share of Sydney's housing growth while other parts of the city have barely changed," he said.

"We can't keep pushing all of Sydney's growth to the west and the urban fringe while established suburbs close to jobs, transport and services are locked away from new housing.

"We're not asking Woollahra to solve the housing crisis on its own. We're asking Woollahra to make a fair contribution, just as we're asking communities right across Sydney to do."

What does the plan include?

The proposal includes about 3.5 hectares of new and upgraded open space across 13 parks, a new Edgecliff plaza and up to nine kilometres of walking and cycling connections.

The government says 95% of new homes would be within 400 metres of open space measuring at least 3000 square metres. It has also committed to no net loss of overall tree canopy within the precinct.

The plan calls for studio, one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments, with at least 3% of the total homes reserved as affordable housing. On certain sites, this proportion could increase to up to 15% in p
title: The 9400-Home Rezoning Plan Set to Shake Up Sydney's East
author: Real Estate Australia

A private developer who grew up in a housing commission home in Wagga Wagga is attempting to tackle the current housing crisis in Taree one property at a time.

Ahmed Meddine is buying and renovating vandalised former Homes NSW (formerly Department of Housing) properties in Bushland Estate to provide affordable rentals.

Mr Meddine is frustrated by the number of houses that are boarded up and left vacant, becoming vandalised in the process, while the vacancy rate for rentals in Taree is sitting at about 1.2 per cent.

"There's more than 10 houses that are boarded up right now," Mr Meddine said.

Mr Meddine is renovating a property in Hughes Street.

"This property stands out: it was sold once before in disrepair, fixed up, re-tenanted, and then, on the same day the tenants vacated, it was broken into and vandalised before being sold to us," he said.

"We're seeing this pattern repeat across Taree, with ... properties boarded up within a few streets of each other.

"The current cycle is property gets damaged, sold as-is, privately repaired, re-tenanted, and then the cycle repeats. This leaves the repair cost and risk to private developers, while vacant boarded-up homes invite further vandalism and antisocial behaviour."

While private buyers point the finger at the state government for the cycle of disrepair, the reality of Bushland Estate is a complex web of management that makes neighbourhood-wide solutions difficult.

The state government said that Homes NSW-owned properties in Taree are not managed by the department itself, but are subject to transfer arrangements with community housing provider Home in Place.

However, Home in Place's executive manager of operations for the area, Tim Larritt, said the provider had only five vacant properties in the estate, with three boarded up because of insurance claims.

Mr Larritt said these vacancies represented less than 1 per cent of their Mid-Coast portfolio.

"It is important to note only 40 per cent of the properties in the Bushland Estate are managed by Home in Place," Mr Larritt said.

"The remainder are managed directly by private owners and real estate agents, or by the Aboriginal Housing Office."

Homes NSW said the Aboriginal Housing Office has no vacant properties in Taree, and denied having a policy of selling damaged properties "as-is".

Home in Place acknowledged the estate had ongoing issues with vandalism.

Mr Larritt said the area faced challenges consistent with many high-density social housing communities, including incidents of antisocial behaviour and third-party property damage.

He said these issues were managed through established tenancy practices and collaboration with NSW Police, Corrective Services and community agencies.

Mr Larritt declined to reveal the total financial cost the vandalism was taking on the public system. He said Home in Place did not provide a running dollar figure for repair costs over the past year because individual incidents varied significantly and an
title: Former public housing kid restores vandalised homes to fix rental crunch

Renters are 16% more likely to experience race and ethnicity discrimination in Europe than in North America, according to new research published this week from the VUB and UGent. The results are based on an analysis of field tests from over half a million rental applications.

The difference comes down to the higher levels of racial diversity in US cities, which means a larger share of both landlords and tenants are likely to be non-white compared to Europe. Additionally, protective legislation has been in place longer in the US, Professor Pieter-Paul Verhaeghe, one of the researchers from the VUB, told The Brussels Times.

"Anti-discrimination legislation in the US is much older than in Europe, dating back to the Fair Housing Act of 1968 (in comparison with the more recent 2000 EU Racial Equality Directive). Moreover, many legal testing measures where implemented in the US, mainly during the late 1980s and during the 1990s. This paid off with less discrimination as a consequence."

Despite protections being in place in both Europe and North America, the study found that rental discrimination has barely changed since the 2000s. Only in one area - socio-economic status - has discrimination seen a fall.

Unia, the public agency with a mandate to combat discrimination, suggested that part of the challenge in Belgium is due to the shortage of housing and the use of social media to post adverts. This makes tracking and taking action difficult, as adverts often do not have the address.

"The housing crisis and the shortage of affordable rental housing play a significant role," Anne Salmon, a spokesperson with Unia, told The Brussels Times.

"The combination of limited supply and high demand from tenants (for example, in Brussels, 62% of residents are tenants) allows landlords to be extremely selective, and sometimes even discriminatory," she said. "The intense competition for available housing makes such discrimination almost impossible to detect."

Rental discrimination still common for some groups

Across all countries, the researchers found that the groups most frequently discriminated against when looking for rental accommodation are ethnic minorities, people with disabilities and those with insecure employment. On average these groups are 20% less likely to be invited to view a home by landlords or estate agents.

"When people think of rental discrimination, the focus quickly turns to ethnic origin. Our study shows that this is indeed one of the main grounds for discrimination, but that people with disabilities or in a precarious socio-economic position are affected just as severely. This reinforces inequality in our society," explained Verhaeghe.

Over 100 field experiments conducted between 2002 to 2024 in 31 different countries were analysed to find common patterns across countries. Field tests see researchers sending multiple applications to real rental adverts, changing nothing between the applications except areas where discrimination is bei
title: Europe worse than North America for race discrimination in renting
author: brusselstimes.com

content:
The revelation by the Executive Secretary of the Tertiary Education Trust Fund (TETFund), Sonny Echono, that about 80 per cent of building materials used in Nigeria are imported should be a wake-up call to policymakers, researchers and industry stakeholders.

For a country struggling with a huge housing deficit, rising construction costs, unemployment and persistent foreign exchange pressures, such dependence is not merely an industrial weakness; it is a serious economic liability.

Nigeria cannot realistically achieve affordable housing or sustainable infrastructure development while much of what is required to construct homes, schools, hospitals, offices and other public facilities continues to come from abroad. Every imported door, window, tile, electrical component and other construction material represents an opportunity that could have been captured by Nigerian manufacturers, entrepreneurs and workers.

Echono's intervention is therefore timely. More importantly, it should trigger a deliberate national programme to reduce import dependence through research, innovation and industrial development.

Nigeria is not short of raw materials. The country possesses abundant deposits of clay, limestone, laterite, sand, timber and other resources that can support the production of a wide range of construction materials. It also has universities, polytechnics, research institutes, architects, engineers and other professionals capable of developing solutions suited to local conditions.

The problem is that research too often remains within academic institutions without making the difficult journey from laboratories to factories and construction sites. This disconnect needs to end. Research funding should not be judged merely by the number of papers published or conferences attended. Increasingly, the test should be whether research produces practical solutions to Nigeria's most pressing problems. Building-material research is one area where such an approach can have immediate economic and social benefits.

TETFund, with its mandate to support tertiary education and research, is strategically positioned to facilitate this transition. It can encourage universities and researchers to develop affordable, durable and climate-responsive alternatives to imported construction products. But research should be undertaken in partnership with manufacturers, construction companies, professional bodies and government agencies so that successful innovations can be commercialised.

The construction industry offers enormous opportunities for local industrialisation. Housing alone generates demand for cement, roofing materials, doors, windows, tiles, sanitary fittings, electrical components, paints, insulation products and numerous other items. If these products can be produced competitively in Nigeria, the multiplier effect on employment and economic activity would be considerable.

There is also a foreign exchange dimension. Nigeria has spent substantial resources impo
title: Break the costly addiction to imported building materials
author: The Guardian

content:
NEW DELHI: The Satya Niketan building collapse has yet again brought Delhi University's long-standing student housing crisis into focus, with accommodation demand far outstripping the university's hostel capacity.

DU's 2024-25 annual report records more than 2.45 lakh regular students, while the university has only 18 hostels, highlighting the sharp mismatch between the number of students and available campus accommodation. The university acknowledges that hostels cannot be guaranteed to all applicants, leaving a vast majority of students to find housing outside the campus.

Over the years, student accommodation clusters have expanded in areas such as Satya Niketan, Munirka and Moti Bagh, out of necessity rather than choice. For students, renting an independent apartment, often costing '20,000 or more a month, is unaffordable.

They instead opt for shared PG rooms costing around '5,000-6,000 per bed, per month. The situation is stark in South Campus. Of the 18 colleges in the area, only three, including Lady Shri Ram College, Sri Venkateswara College and Maitreyi College, provide hostel accommodation on campus.

Students from the remaining South Campus colleges are largely dependent on private facilities. For outstation students, finding accommodation close to college is a challenge and hence they choose any shared accommodation simply to remain within walking distance of their colleges.
title: Delhi building collapse: Many students, too few rooms
author: The New Indian Express

content:
As rents run into tens of thousands of rupees, Satya Niketan students have little idea who their landlords and who is ultimately responsible for the condition of the property.

For thousands of students living in Delhi's Satya Niketan - the place which has been under the spotlight after a five-storey building collapsed on Sunday, killing seven students - finding a paying guest accommodation often means dealing with brokers and middlemen rather than the people who actually own the buildings.

Even as rents run into tens of thousands of rupees, many students say they have little idea who their landlords are, where they can be contacted or who is ultimately responsible for the condition of the property.

As the owners remain invisible, the power falls into the hands of the middlemen who provide students with the accommodation and then become their only lifeline to deal with any crisis in the PG.

This results in students living in poor conditions, facing water shortages daily and dealing with unthinkable difficulties with no one to answer their questions.

'Broken Walls, Owner Unknown': Tenants Of Collapsed Building Narrate Ordeal

Speaking to CNN-News18, Yashwanth Vemanand Reddy Reddam, a former tenant of the Satya Niketan building that collapsed, said he lived there in 2024 but left when renovation work was planned.

"Actually, I stayed in the Satya Niketan building, which has collapsed now, in 2024 and later vacated because they wanted to renovate. When I stayed, only the top floor was in better condition. The rest of the 3 floors were too old, and they were vacant because living in those rooms was horrible: broken walls, narrow stairs that were very badly maintained. There was no proper maintenance of the building, firstly. And we don't know who the owner was. We just knew the middlemen," he said.

Reddy said parts of the building were already in poor condition when renovation work began.

"Also, the first and second floors were already broken, and so they started to renovate, and they made it and hiked the rent prices, and finally collapsed, and innocent lives were lost," he added.

Habib, another tenant who was currently living in the building but survived because of his absence during its collapse, said the property had been made to look much better despite its underlying condition.

"I had to reach building in evening.. they had painted it so well nobody had guessed it is in such dire conditions....rent was 16k for one bed.. so total 32K.. didnt know who the owner was.. was only aware about the third party.. they used to solve our problems... water supply was an issue.. Food was bad," he said, while speaking to CNN-News18.

'Lack Of Direct Contact With Owner Rampant In Satya Niketan'

The lack of direct contact with property owners appears to be a wider concern among students living in the area.

Nirali, a student living in Satya Niketan, said that most of the time, owners don't live here and tenants have no idea who they are.

"Most of the
title: 'Nobody Knew The Owner': Students Paid Rs 32,000 Rent To Live Amid Broken Walls In Collapsed Delhi PG

There are a range of one to three bedroom homes available in this phase of the development and the homes will be ready before the end of the year

Applications will open this week for a number of cost rental properties at Folkstown Park, Balbriggan, Co Dublin.

The properties are part of Phase 2 of the cost rental portion of the development. There are a range of one to three bedroom homes available.

24 cost rental homes in total are becoming available, and will be ready from late November or early December 2026. There are two 1-bedroom duplexes measuring 53 m², which rent for €1,100 per month.

Additionally, twelve 2-bedroom mid-terrace houses measuring 74 m² are available for €1,400 per month. For 3-bedroom properties, the development offers four mid-terrace houses measuring 130 m² at €1,575.

Two duplex apartments measuring 117 m² are available for €1,600, and four end-terrace houses measuring 130 m² with a rent of €1,695.00.

The properties feature a modern, low-maintenance exterior façade built to high energy-efficiency standards with an A-rating. Inside, each home boasts a bright, well-presented layout with modern design, tasteful interior finishes, and flooring included throughout.

Kitchens come fully fitted with white goods included, while the bathrooms offer modern finishes with partial tiling.

For heating and electrical, the homes use sustainable and renewable energy technology, including an energy-efficient heat pump system to achieve a minimum A2 BER rating. High levels of insulation and airtightness enhance comfort while reducing environmental impact, alongside generous lighting, power points, and switches throughout.

The location provides convenient access to nearby amenities, sitting just a 5-minute drive from both Balbriggan town centre and Balbriggan Beach. Additionally, Ardgillan Castle is a 10-minute drive away, Millfield Shopping Centre is a 15-minute walk, and Dublin City Centre can be reached in 45 minutes by car.

For motorists, the development is ideally situated for commuting and regional travel, offering a short drive to both Dublin and Drogheda along with easy access to the M1, M50, and N2 road networks.

Public transport links are equally accessible, highlighted by a 7-minute cycle to Balbriggan Train Station. Residents can take advantage of regular train services to Dublin City Centre, as well as frequent bus routes running into the city.

Cost Rental guarantees rent prices at least 25% below local market rates. It is aimed at people who have a net household income of €66,000 or below.

Applications for Folkstown Park (Phase 2) open on Friday, 11 September at 2PM. The application closing date will be announced 7 days prior to closing. You can find more information here.
title: Applications open for Balbriggan cost rental homes from €1,100 for a duplex
author: Dublin Live

SHREVEPORT, La. (KTAL/KMSS) - Higher gas prices are affecting drivers this Labor Day, prompting some to change their travel plans and look for ways to save money at the pump.

For Bre'Tavious Jones, higher gas prices are forcing him to stay home with his family.

"Gas prices high, rent prices high. If you got a mortgage, mortgage high. Everything high. Food high," Jones said. "We really don't have it like that. We don't have all that to be trying to go and fill up and do this and go get food."

According to AAA, the national average price for regular gasoline is $4.14 per gallon, compared with $3.20 a year ago. The national average has never been above $4 per gallon on Labor Day.

Jones said the higher prices have him finding ways to stretch his gas money.

"I have every app possible to save money on gas," Jones said. "When you shop at the grocery store, you have different discounts and rewards and stuff that you get when you shop there."

Jones said he uses rewards to save at the pump; he noted that even a 10-cent discount can add up.

Diesel prices are also costing drivers more. AAA said diesel hit a record high, with a national average of $5.89 per gallon.

One driver said those costs can create an added expense for people who own trucks or have to cover costs upfront while waiting to be reimbursed.

AAA said gasoline demand typically drops this time of year, which can help bring prices down. However, higher oil costs are leading to changes for drivers.
title: High fuel costs force Shreveport residents to stay home
author: WNTZ - cenlanow.com

Registering to vote in Michigan is simple and can be done online, by mail, or in person, depending on how close you are to Election Day.

One year into President Donald Trump's second term, the waves of policy change are reverberating in Wayne County. In Detroit, first-time homeowner Tamika Simley is trying to hold it all together, juggling mortgage payments, groceries, gas, and utilities on a budget that keeps getting tighter.

"You're having to pick and choose between things, and you shouldn't have to," Simley said in an interview earlier this year. "Why should I have to choose between my rent or my mortgage and feeding my family?"

While Simley's story is personal, it reflects a much broader struggle now facing thousands of Wayne County residents as federal policy shifts take hold.

Though some of the steepest cuts do not fully kick in until 2027, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed by President Trump in 2025, slashes funding and imposes stricter eligibility limits for SNAP and Medicaid. Combined with changes to federal housing programs and increased housing costs, experts say strained budgets could affect housing stability for some Wayne County families.

Supporters of the OBBBA say the changes are intended to reduce federal spending, tighten eligibility requirements, and encourage workforce participation in public assistance programs.

But in a county where many rent and the poverty rate far exceeds the state average, local officials warn these federal cuts will force thousands of residents to make impossible choices to remain in stable housing. As Michigan heads into pivotal midterms, state and local governments are scrambling to fill the gaps left by the federal government.

Julie Cassidy, a senior policy analyst at the Michigan League for Public Policy focusing on the social determinants of health, cites the change in housing costs as a main concern - especially rising rent prices, as more than one-third of households rent in Wayne County compared to 27% statewide.

According to federal guidelines, housing is considered affordable if it costs no more than 30 percent of a household's income. But in Wayne County, many are far beyond that limit.

"We consistently find in every community that renters are having to spend a lot more of their income on rent than homeowners do, and their housing costs are increasing more quickly. In Wayne, the median rent is 38 percent of the median household income," said Cassidy.

U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Detroit, who recently lost a bid for re-election in a district with one of the nation's highest poverty rates, said earlier this year his constituents are acutely aware of how federal policy is hitting their pocketbooks.

Life has become more expensive in Trump's tenure, Thanedar said. "He says he's going to work on lowering costs, and he talked about inflation. He said that he alone can fix all that, because he is such an economic genius. In reality, prices have gone up substantially, and housing
title: For low-income Michiganders, federal changes could land on housing
author: Detroit Free Press

Easing demand and slower sales push Perth's stock of homes for sale to a three-year high

By Mina Martin

Perth's property market is showing clearer signs of rebalancing, with the number of homes advertised for sale reaching 7,335 at the end of August -- the highest total since March 2023.

The figure was up 7.8% on July and a striking 146.1% higher than the same time last year, reflecting how thin listings had become over the past two years.

REIWA president Suzanne Brown (pictured) said the jump reflected softer buyer demand rather than a sudden wave of new sellers.

"Active listings have more than doubled since March," Brown said, adding that new listings had "mostly returned to long-term average levels" after a shortage in late 2025 and early 2026.

She said the added stock represented "an easing in demand, which has led to a decline in sales activity," driven in part by three interest rate rises that have squeezed borrowing power and mortgage serviceability, alongside changes to federal tax policy that have cooled both investor and first-home buyer activity.

Those hikes brought the cash rate to 4.35%, where the RBA has now held for a second consecutive meeting, with governor Michele Bullock signalling the board is still watching for further inflation progress before considering any change of direction.

Brown cautioned that these annual figures lag behind current conditions.

"REIWA's annual median sale prices are currently showing some growth, but when we look at the June 2026 quarter, Perth's median sale prices have recorded declines," she said, noting most suburbs posted quarterly price falls.

Time on market has also stretched, with houses taking a median 23 days to sell in August, 12 days slower than a year earlier, and units taking 21 days, 11 days slower annually.

Brown said Perth's rental supply "continues to be low," warning that reduced investor lending activity in the June quarter, per ABS and bank data, was "a concern for rental supply, vacancy rates, and rent prices going forward."

title: Perth listings break 7,000 for first time since 2023

An old fishing shack on one of Wynnum's best streets has sold for $1.82 million, snapped up in a pre-auction deal by the deceased owner's granddaughter.

The rugged two-bedroom cottage features a cold room for the daily catch and a 923-square-metre block just metres from the waterfront at 11 Alkoomie Street.

While it was built in the '70s, the land has remained in the hands of pioneer fishing family the Castners for four generations.

After her pre-auction offer was accepted last week, that legacy is set to live on for a fifth.

The Wynnum shack was one of 128 scheduled auctions across South East Queensland over the past week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary clearance rate of 17 per cent from 90 reported results, with five homes withdrawn.

The "weak" auction figures follow fresh reports Brisbane dwelling values dipped in August.

AMP chief economist Dr Shane Oliver said the Queensland capital had been "whacked" by poor affordability, predicting prices to fall as much as 15 per cent in the coming year.

"Brisbane is getting hit hard because it's coming off the top of a massive boom where prices surged dramatically and that has left the market vulnerable," he said.

"And it's gotten a bit worse because of the likelihood of more rate rises and the ongoing tax issues with investors."

Cotality figures for August revealed Brisbane dwelling prices fell 1 per cent to $1,080,142.

Given Brisbane property prices doubled in the space of a few years during the pandemic-era boom, Oliver said the fall was far from disastrous and called the price correction inevitable.

Gaby McEwan of McGrath Wynnum, who put away the historic Alkoomie Street deal, said about 28 groups inspected the home throughout the auction campaign.

"We didn't get a huge amount of interest but that's the market right now," she said.

"I think the bottom end of the market has taken a big smack because all the investors are dumping their properties and first-home buyers are stretched at a million dollars.

"I'm seeing a 10 per cent drop in property prices now."

For the Castner family, however, the pre-auction sale delivered a fairytale ending.

"This parcel has been in the family for well over 100 years - they're a legendary fishing family in the area," she said.

"Bert Castner built the home in the '70s but he actually grew up in the house next door - at 15 Alkoomie - which also remains in the family.

"It's a small but wonderfully tangible piece of Wynnum's old fishing history ... and now it's beginning another chapter in Castner hands."

McEwan said the young family would restore the home.

"That whole area is being gentrified and until a few weeks ago that street had the highest-recorded sale price in the suburb at $4,005,000," she said.

In Indooroopilly, a 1920s Queenslander on a 1017-square-metre block at 11 Essex Road sold for $2.525 million to a young upsizing family bidding over the phone from Stradbroke Island.

They were the sole bidders on the property, whi
title: Granddaughter snaps up historic fishing shack for $1.82 million
author: The Sydney Morning Herald

Garry Bridges was elected as the new leader of Manchester City Council this week.

New Manchester City Council leader Garry Bridges has revealed his 'top priority' for the city - and shared his plans to address issues such as rising rent prices which are making life difficult for thousands of Mancunians.

In his first interview since being appointed council leader on Thursday night, Councillor Bridges told the Manchester Evening News (MEN) how he wants to see Manchester change, spoke about his plans for Strangeways prison, and admitted which football team he supports.

He responded to the possibility of him losing his seat in the Old Moat ward next year after the Green Party won the area in this May's local elections, and said that Manchester needs to 'push developers to have more affordable housing in all and every development' in the city.

Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter

The new leader was voted by Labour councillors this week as the successor to Bev Craig who was elected as Greater Manchester mayor in July.

Asked what his message would be for the corners of Manchester which feel left behind from the city's success, Garry Bridges said: "The message from me is that those places that have felt left behind are my top priority, that is literally what we're here to do.

"I can see why you would look around the city and feel that way. Because of the way that the government has been structured over the last 20 years, what we've been able to deliver has been about us harnessing the market effectively, and so, naturally, that leads you to a place where the city centre leads the wave on that - but that's not enough."

The new leader said while the council has 'already got big plans' for regeneration in the city, it is 'just not enough' and issued a promise to residents that they 'will start to see improvements in future years'.

Councillor Bridges' appointment as council leader this week sees him left in charge of a city with a £1bn budget which provides services for the 600,000 people who call Manchester home.

But the new boss has plenty of headaches to worry about too.

A council report in March revealed stark issues over housing, with 59 people sleeping rough - the highest amount since 2024. The document also shared that there are more families staying in emergency housing than 12 months ago.

Rent prices are on the up too, described as being 'sky-high' by the housing and homelessness charity, Shelter.

What is the new leader's plan to fix these problems?

"Rents are too high, and I think everyone knows that there's a huge problem with rents," the council leader said.

"If you look at the percentage of people's income that they spend on housing now, it's completely out of kilter, and people will really struggle to make ends meet as a result.

"We think that one of the main ways that we can change that is by large-scale intervention by building social housing at scale. That's one of the tools tha
title: Meet Manchester council's new leader - what he's got planned for the city
author: Manchester Evening News

There is a place in New York City that many insist does not exist. It is primarily composed of concrete streets, old family-run stores, and a massive influx of newer, sleeker businesses with scrawled cursive logos and $7 drinks. It is called "East Willliamsburg."

East Williamsburg, depending on who you ask, could be anything. Its geographical boundaries are contentious and ever-debated, since it has not been historically defined by government agencies, and there are no official neighborhood lines drawn, but the name has been used vaguely to refer to an industrial area of Williamsburg that developers have been trying to revitalize since at least the 1980s. For longtime residents, the neighborhood itself is about as real as Santa Claus, or the tooth fairy -- "East Williamsburg" could've just as easily been "South Greenpoint" or "West Bushwick" or "Tatooine" or "Six Flags." But for many, especially people who have just landed in Brooklyn, it is a very real place. More specifically, it's a playground. East Williamsburg is a sprawling obstacle course of shops and bars, all catering to the younger new residents who have moved to New York City in order to work hard and play harder.

I have heard from haggard, decrepit millennials that it used to be different, that it used to be grungy and alternative. That's not the Williamsburg I know. I know a Williamsburg where there's not just one, but two Whole Foods, and one of them is a combination building with a Capital One bank. Gwyneth Paltrow is allegedly opening a Goop store, too. I know it as the "most exciting Asian American coffee hotspot," which is a title that I feel represents both a very cool thing happening for sprouting businesses and sometimes also the fourth horseman of the apocalypse. While the neighborhood used to be renowned for flannel-clad IPA connoisseurs and a thriving indie art scene, the 2010s-era hipsters who sparked the Hasidim vs. Hipsters war have now been usurped by a new stereotype: the tech bro.

It wasn't always this way. For decades, the wider area of Williamsburg has held a major cultural fascination for the type of millennial transplant who makes their way out to the East Coast. Williamsburg is the setting for the 2010s CBS sitcom 2 Broke Girls, the story of how a billionaire's daughter had to flee to Brooklyn after losing all her money and start over again in a diner. It's where Dakota Johnson apparently lives while going through her post-college identity crisis in the 2010s breakup movie How to Be Single. Williamsburg is the secret fourth girl in Lena Dunham's HBO show Girls, so consistently featured on screen that there are Sex in the City-style crawls of all the North Brooklyn businesses that appear in the show. Former Teen Vogue editor-in-chief Elaine Welteroth wrote, about moving to the newly minted East Williamsburg to chase her big magazine dre
title: An Infamous New York Neighborhood Has Entered a Bizarre New Phase
author: Slate Magazine

Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The average cost of houses across the West Midlands have been revealed in a new report.

The West Midlands State of the Region 2026 report sets out the cost of buying and renting properties in Birmingham, Coventry, Dudley, Sandwell, Solihull, Walsall and Wolverhampton.

And the findings show home ownership continues to be less affordable than previous years.

The report will be presented to members of the West Midlands Combined Authority's Local Scrutiny Committee when it meets on Monday, September 7.

It said the average cost of buying houses varies across the WMCA area with the most expensive being in Solihull at £329,000 and the lowest being Sandwell at £200,000.

The average house price in Birmingham is £233,000, £227,000 in Dudley, £226,000 in Coventry, £216,000 in Walsall and £213,000 in Wolverhampton.

Affordability also varies across the region with the median house price being between 8.62 and 5.86 times the average wage in 2024 compared with 7.16 and 4.83 in 2014.

The highest house price to wage ratio is 8.62 in Solihull while Coventry is the lowest with 5.86.

The ratio in Birmingham is 6.01, in Dudley it is 6.53, in Sandwell is 6.39, in Walsall it's 6.16 and in Wolverhampton is 5.90.

Average monthly rent prices are also highest in Solihull at £1,252 with the lowest being £846 in Dudley.

In Birmingham, the average rent price is at £1,087, in Coventry it's £1,016, in Sandwell it's £936, in Wolverhampton it's £921 and in Walsall it's £898.

The average proportion of household income spent on rent across local authorities of the WMCA area was estimated at 29.6 per cent in 2023/24.

This varies from 36.1 per cent in Solihull to 26.6 per cent in Wolverhampton.

Weekly incomes after housing costs vary from £180.68 in Sandwell to £294.12 in Solihull, in the financial year ending 2023.

In Walsall income after housing costs is at £211.78, in Birmingham it's £209.05, in Dudley it's £208.89, in Coventry it's £206.70 and in Wolverhampton it's £181.95.

The report said: "Housing is central to improving quality of life, supporting regeneration, and delivering inclusive growth across the West Midlands.

"Outcomes for the region and its communities can be improved by making it easier for people to access safe, affordable, and well‐located homes that support healthier, more secure lives."
title: Not Dudley or Walsall - the most affordable place to buy a house in the West Midlands
author: Yahoo News UK

It's last call for the original Pappasitos.

Courtesy of Pappasitos

Editor's note: It's time to look back at the top Houston news of the week, from a Tex-Mex institution's impending closure to all the best steak nights in town. Read on for our most popular stories, then plan your Labor Day weekend right here.

1. Houston Tex-Mex institution's original location to close after 43 years. The original location of a pioneering Houston Tex-Mex restaurant will soon serve its last order of fajitas. Pappasitos Cantina is closing its location at Richmond and Hillcroft on September 13.

2. 12 special Houston steak nights served Monday through Thursday. Houstonians love a deal, especially when it involves a juicy steak. Thankfully, Houston's bars and restaurants are serving up a host of compelling steak night specials.

3. 2 Michelin-rated Houston restaurants teamed up for taco-fueled fundraiser. Held Sunday, August 30, the Perfect Pairing event united Tatemó chef-owner Emmanuel Chavez with The Pit Room's Memorial location for an epic evening of tacos, margaritas, and community.

4. Award-winning Houston smash burger restaurant sets Katy opening date. The wait is nearly over for the eagerly anticipated Katy location of Burger Bodega. The smash hit smash burger concept will open at 11 am on September 19.

5. Houston home to No. 2 biggest drop in rent prices in U.S. since last year. A new report has revealed that Texas is leading the nation in annual rent declines since 2025, and Houston rent prices have fallen as much as 14 percent since last August.
title: Houston Tex-Mex institution to close flagship and more popular stories

Strict rules limiting platforms like Airbnb have slowed the rate of rent increases across Canadian cities, saving local tenants tens of dollars each month, according to research examining six years of national housing data.

The findings, published in a joint study by McGill University Professor David Wachsmuth and University of Waterloo postdoctoral researcher Cloé St-Hilaire, provide concrete empirical proof linking short-term rental restrictions to reduced rental inflation.

"We found absolute, iron-clad evidence that short-term rental regulations put downward pressure on rent," Wachsmuth, the study's lead researcher, said in a statement. "Lots of things cause housing to be expensive, but this is low-hanging fruit to manage those costs."

The City of Vancouver acted as a pioneer in 2018 when it limited short-term listings strictly to primary residences, preventing hosts from running secondary units like basement suites or laneway houses as full-time vacation rentals. British Columbia expanded similar restrictions provincewide in 2024.

A measurable drop in monthly rent prices

While housing experts and residents long assumed short-term platforms drove up prices by removing long-term housing supply, the researchers set out to verify whether restrictions actually cooled local markets.

By comparing cities with primary residence restrictions against municipalities that allowed unrestricted vacation listings, the study revealed a clear divergence in rental price trajectories.

Before the rules came in, rents in cities with lots of vacation rentals were rising about as fast as they were elsewhere in Canada. But once cities started limiting short-term rentals to people's primary homes, rent increases began to slow compared with places that didn't have those restrictions.

* Lagos can be quite stressful when searching for affordable accommodation in the city

* Some residents in the city, with an estimated population of 21 million, have been complaining about the skyrocketing rent in the state

* However, some locations offer relief for price-sensitive renters, whose budgets are slim and lean

Pascal Oparada is a journalist with Legit.ng, covering technology, energy, stocks, investment, and the economy for over a decade.

Finding affordable accommodation in Lagos has become increasingly difficult, but renters working with limited budgets may still find better options outside the city's most expensive neighbourhoods.

Ikorodu is emerging as one of the areas where tenants can find relatively cheaper accommodation, with current property listings showing self-contained apartments and mini-flats available at prices below what many renters may encounter in more central parts of Lagos.

Recent listings show that a self-contained apartment in Ikorodu can be found from around ₦300,000 to ₦400,000 per year, although prices vary considerably depending on the location, building and facilities.

Nigeria Property Centre currently puts the average asking price for self-contained apartments in the area at about ₦400,000 annually.

Mini-flats from about ₦500,000

For tenants who want more space than a single-room self-contained apartment, Ikorodu also has room-and-parlour mini-flats.

Current listings include mini-flats around ₦500,000 to ₦800,000 per year, while the average asking price for mini-flats is around ₦700,000 annually.

Some listings can be cheaper, depending on the particular neighbourhood and condition of the property.

Areas within Ikorodu such as Igbogbo, Gberigbe, Agric, Isawo, Jumofak and Oreyo feature in current rental listings, giving prospective tenants several locations to consider.

What about two-bedroom apartments?

Ikorodu becomes more expensive when tenants move into two-bedroom apartments, but it can still offer options for households looking beyond the smaller units.

Current listings include two-bedroom flats for about ₦700,000 to ₦1.5 million per year, while Nigeria Property Centre's August 2026 market data puts the average price at approximately ₦1.2 million annually.

The same data shows prices ranging from ₦350,000 to ₦3 million, highlighting how widely rents can differ across properties.

Cheap rent does not mean cheap living

For tenants considering Ikorodu, rent should not be the only factor.

The distance from some parts of Ikorodu to workplaces, schools and businesses elsewhere in Lagos can mean higher transportation costs and longer journeys.

A cheaper apartment may therefore make less financial sense if a tenant spends significantly more commuting every day.

Tenants should also remember that the advertised rent may not represent the full amount required before moving in.

title: N300,000 and up: 6 Lagos neighbourhoods to consider If rent is breaking your budget

The average rent in existing tenancies across Kerry's six Local Electoral Areas is above €900 a month.

That's according to the Residential Tenancies Board report for the first quarter of 2026.

It shows the average standardised rent in the county jumped by over 5% in a year.

According to the RTB report, nationally, rent prices for new tenancies have increased by over 9% since last year.

Kerry was among six counties in Ireland which saw the lowest rental inflation in the second quarter of 2026.

The average rent for new tenancies in the county between January and March was €1,311 a month.

That's a 5% rise in a year; and a quarter-on-quarter increase of 5.4%.

Rent for existing tenancies jumped by 6.7% in twelve months, to €1,048 per month; a quarter-on-quarter rise of almost 3%.

The figures show that Tralee is the most expensive area in the county to rent a new tenancy, at an average of €1,405 a month.

In Killarney it's €1,285; €1,237 is the average cost of rent for a new tenancy in Kenmare, while it's €1,222 a month in the Listowel LEA.

Data for new tenancies in the Castleisland and Corca Dhuibhne areas was not listed in the report.

Rents for existing tenancies in the county are all over €900 a month, with Killarney the most expensive at €1,178, followed by Tralee at €1,056.

An existing tenancy in both the Castleisland (€957) and Kenmare (€956) areas is just over €955 monthly, while rent in the Listowel (€932) and Corca Dhuibhne (€929) LEA's are approximately €930 a month.
title: Average rent in Kerry ranged between over €1,000-€1,300 a month in first quarter of 2026 | RadioKerry.ie
author: RadioKerry.ie

Whippy wars as ice-cream business forced to relocate

The owner of an ice-cream business said he is prepared to go to court after being frozen out by the council who awarded the lease of his current unit to someone else, forcing him to relocate.

Dan Harding, of Dan's Delights, has complained to Portsmouth City Council after he was outbid for his unit in College Park, Copnor, which has been his business's home for the past six years.

The 37-year-old told The News how rent prices for the unit have risen from £300 to £650 in the past three years, with soaring prices of stock and staff wages meaning he was unable to meet the expected rates to retain the site.

Dan is now having to scout out new locations to operate from, prompting him to launch a GoFundMe to raise £10,000 which will fund the refit of a new building which will serve as a hub for the business.

He said: "I asked for a ten-year lease and they said they would discuss it. I wanted to make my staff jobs more secure and offer them stability and some for the company as well because we invested quite a lot of money there because it wasn't very good when we first got there. We have really made it a community hub and I pushed for a decision but was told that it was going up for tender and I thought that was unfair.

"It was all about money. I don't know how much the person who won bid. I bid £500 because it wasn't worth it - we have had to go out and around to make sure we had staff wages, the money just isn't there. We've had a horrendous year this year. We only make money from April to October and then the customers we get come because of our page.

"We lost the tender because someone bid more but they said it isn't about the money, but it is. The council is in a position of power and they aren't transparent or fair. It's supposed to be a point scoring system but it's when it suits and there is no fixed policy with the council and it's how they see fit. I've put in a complaint and some questions but I'm willing to do a judicial review. I will take them to court if need be."

A hairdressers in Copnor has piqued the interest of the owner, who said, if his plans are successful, it will require a complete makeover, with the money going towards a refurbishment, the installation of existing equipment, setup costs and staff wages.

He continued: "We have got to move into a new site and we've seen one that is currently a hairdressers but it will be an ice cream parlour so the money will be for a refit so it's going to go towards that."

The fundraiser, which has secured £125, said: "We are incredibly disappointed by the way this situation has been handled and by the lack of support and empathy we have received. After six years of building our business, serving the community and providing employment, we have suddenly been left without a premises.But we don't want this to be the end of our story. We need your help to raise £10,000.

"Starting again is daunting, but we are determined to do it. If you
title: 'I will take them to court': Ice cream business hits out over lease dispute
